name: Aliskiren
usedFor: Treatment of hypertension (high blood pressure) in adults.
howItWorks: Blocks a substance in the body that helps raise blood pressure. This helps blood vessels relax and lowers blood pressure.
adverseEffects: Swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat
warnings: Extra caution is needed for people with kidney problems, diabetes, dehydration or low blood pressure. Certain combinations with other blood pressure medicines can increase the risk of kidney problems and high potassium.
olderAdultSafety: Older adults may be more sensitive to low blood pressure and may have reduced kidney function. Blood tests may be needed to check kidney function and potassium levels.
caregiverGuidance: Help the older adult take the medicine as prescribed. Keep scheduled blood tests. Do not give potassium supplements or potassium-based salt substitutes unless the healthcare provider approves them. If the person feels dizzy, help them sit down. Seek emergency help for swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing.

name: Amlodipine
usedFor: Treats high blood pressure and chest pain from coronary artery disease (angina).
howItWorks: Blocks calcium from entering the muscle cells of the blood vessels and heart. The blood vessels relax and widen, which lowers blood pressure and eases the heart's workload.
commonSideEffects: Swelling of the ankles or feet
adverseEffects: Worsening chest pain or heart attack (rare, mostly in people with severe blocked heart arteries when treatment starts or the dose goes up)
Severe allergic reaction with swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat
Liver problems (yellowing of the skin or eyes)
warnings: Ankle swelling, dizziness and low blood pressure are the most common problems. Use with caution in people with severe aortic stenosis, heart failure or liver disease. Do not stop it suddenly without asking the doctor, because blood pressure may go up again. Tell the doctor or pharmacist before adding other medicines, since some (for example, simvastatin) need a lower dose when taken with amlodipine.
olderAdultSafety: Older adults clear amlodipine more slowly, so a lower starting dose (2.5 mg) is often used. Older adults are more prone to dizziness, ankle swelling and falls, and any new or worsening swelling should be checked by a healthcare professional.
caregiverGuidance: Give with or without food. Check blood pressure and pulse as the doctor directs, and help the older adult stand up slowly. Look at the ankles and feet daily and report new or worsening swelling. Report dizziness, fainting, or chest pain that is new or worse. Seek emergency help for chest pain that does not go away, fainting, or swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat.

name: Atenolol
usedFor: Treats high blood pressure and angina (chest pain). It is also used early after a heart attack to improve survival.
howItWorks: Blocks beta-1 receptors in the heart, so the heart beats more slowly and with less force. This lowers blood pressure and the heart's workload.
adverseEffects: Chest pain, irregular heartbeat or heart attack if stopped suddenly. It can hide the fast heartbeat that warns of low blood sugar in people with diabetes
warnings: The label carries a boxed warning: do not stop it suddenly, especially in people with coronary artery disease, because chest pain or a heart attack can occur. Atenolol is cleared mainly by the kidneys, so the dose must be lowered when kidney function is reduced. Use with caution in asthma or lung disease, heart failure, diabetes and thyroid disease. Tell the surgeon or dentist before any procedure.
olderAdultSafety: Older adults have about 50% lower total clearance and higher blood levels, and that dosing should start at the low end (for example, 25 mg daily in some older adults being treated for high blood pressure) because kidney function declines with age. Watch for a pulse that is too slow, dizziness on standing, tiredness, and falls.
caregiverGuidance: Give at about the same time each day. Never stop it suddenly or let the supply run out. Check pulse and blood pressure as the doctor directs, and ask which pulse number means the dose should be held and the doctor called. Help the older adult rise slowly. If the older adult has diabetes, check blood sugar as directed. Report fainting, a very slow pulse, wheezing, shortness of breath, leg swelling, or rapid weight gain. Seek emergency help for chest pain or severe trouble breathing.

name: Atorvastatin
usedFor: Lowers LDL ('bad') cholesterol and triglycerides and reduces the risk of heart attack and stroke in people at risk of heart disease. It does not lower blood pressure, but it is often prescribed together with blood pressure medicines.
howItWorks: Blocks an enzyme the liver uses to make cholesterol, so less cholesterol is made and more is removed from the blood.
commonSideEffects: Pain in the arms or legs
adverseEffects: Rhabdomyolysis (severe muscle pain, weakness and dark urine)
Liver injury (yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, upper stomach pain)
Immune-mediated muscle disease that does not go away after stopping
Memory loss or confusion (reported and reversible)
warnings: Report unexplained muscle pain, tenderness or weakness, especially with fever or dark urine. Liver tests may be checked. Large amounts of grapefruit juice (more than about 1.2 liters daily) can raise levels. Levels also rise with some antibiotics (such as clarithromycin), antifungals, HIV medicines, cyclosporine and gemfibrozil, which can raise the risk of muscle damage.
olderAdultSafety: Age 65 or older as a risk factor for myopathy (muscle damage), together with kidney problems, untreated low thyroid, higher doses and certain interacting medicines. Ask the doctor whether the dose is still appropriate if new muscle pain, weakness or confusion appears.
caregiverGuidance: Give once daily at the same time each day, with or without food. Limit grapefruit juice. Keep lab appointments. Check with the pharmacist before adding any new medicine, including antibiotics and antifungals. Report muscle pain or weakness, dark urine, yellow skin or eyes, or new confusion or memory problems to the doctor. Do not stop it without asking the doctor.

name: Azilsartan
usedFor: Treats high blood pressure in adults.
howItWorks: Blocks angiotensin II, a substance that narrows blood vessels, from acting on the blood vessels. The vessels relax, which lowers blood pressure. Azilsartan medoxomil is a prodrug that is converted to the active azilsartan in the gut during absorption.
adverseEffects: Swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat (angioedema)
warnings: Boxed warning: can cause injury and death to an unborn baby, so it must be stopped when pregnancy is detected. Low blood pressure is more likely with dehydration or salt depletion. Kidney function should be monitored, especially in kidney disease. Do not combine with aliskiren in people with diabetes. NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen) can reduce the effect and worsen kidney function. Lithium levels may rise.
olderAdultSafety: The FDA label notes that abnormally high creatinine values (a kidney marker) were more likely in patients aged 75 or older. The 2023 AGS Beers Criteria recommends avoiding routine use of this medicine together with another renin-angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitor, and avoiding routine use with a potassium-sparing diuretic in older adults with chronic kidney disease Stage 3a or higher, because of the risk of high potassium and kidney injury. Combining it with lithium should generally be avoided or require close monitoring of lithium levels. Older adults are also more prone to dizziness, low blood pressure and falls, so regular blood tests are needed to monitor kidney function and potassium levels.
caregiverGuidance: Give at the same time each day, with or without food. Keep scheduled blood tests. Do not give potassium supplements or potassium-based salt substitutes unless the doctor approves. Ask the doctor or pharmacist before giving ibuprofen or similar pain relievers, or the antibiotic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, because they can affect the kidneys or raise potassium with this medicine. Help the older adult stand up slowly. Call the doctor for vomiting, diarrhea or poor drinking, since dehydration can harm the kidneys. Report dizziness, fainting, or reduced urine. Seek emergency help for swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, or difficulty breathing.

usedFor: Treats high blood pressure (oral tablets). Betaxolol eye drops, used for glaucoma, are a different product.

usedFor: Treats high blood pressure. In some countries it is also prescribed for chronic heart failure, depending on the product. Fumarate is the salt form used in tablets.

name: Bumetanide
usedFor: A strong 'water pill' used to treat swelling (edema) caused by heart failure, liver disease and kidney disease. It is not usually the first choice for high blood pressure.
howItWorks: Blocks the kidneys from taking back salt (sodium and chloride) in the loop of Henle, so more salt and water leave the body as urine. It starts working within 30 to 60 minutes and acts for a few hours.
commonSideEffects: Low potassium, sodium or other electrolytes
adverseEffects: Severe dehydration and low blood volume with very low blood pressure, kidney problems or collapse
Hearing loss or ringing in the ears
Severe allergic reaction (people allergic to sulfonamides may react)
Confusion or coma in people with severe liver disease
warnings: The label carries a boxed warning: it is a potent diuretic that, if given in excessive amounts, can cause profound loss of water and electrolytes, so the dose must be adjusted to each person. Potassium, sodium and kidney function should be checked. Hearing problems are more likely with high doses or with certain antibiotics (aminoglycosides). Use with caution in liver disease, gout and diabetes. It should not be used if the person cannot pass urine (anuria).
olderAdultSafety: The FDA label notes that older adults had lower clearance and a smaller diuretic response, and that too much diuresis can cause dehydration and circulatory collapse, particularly in the elderly. The 2023 AGS Beers Criteria advises using diuretics with caution because they can cause or worsen low sodium (hyponatremia or SIADH); sodium should be checked soon after starting or changing the dose. Lithium levels should be closely monitored if used together. In older women, avoid combining a loop diuretic with an alpha-1 blocker such as doxazosin, prazosin or terazosin, because this may increase the risk of urinary incontinence.
caregiverGuidance: Give in the morning, or as directed, to reduce nighttime trips to the bathroom. Keep the path to the toilet clear and use a night light or bedside commode to prevent falls. If the older adult has heart failure, weigh them at the same time each day and record it. Keep scheduled blood tests. Report confusion, muscle cramps, extreme thirst, dizziness, very little urine, ringing in the ears or hearing changes, rapid weight gain, or new leg swelling. Seek emergency help for fainting or severe weakness.

name: Captopril
usedFor: Treats high blood pressure and heart failure. It is also used after a heart attack in people with reduced heart function and to slow kidney damage in diabetic kidney disease.
howItWorks: Blocks an enzyme that makes angiotensin II, a substance that tightens blood vessels. The blood vessels relax and widen, which lowers blood pressure. Captopril works quickly and wears off within hours, so it is usually taken two to three times a day.
commonSideEffects: Taste changes or loss of taste
adverseEffects: Angioedema (swelling of the face, lips, tongue, throat or limbs)
Low white blood cell count (fever, sore throat, mouth sores)
Large amounts of protein in the urine
warnings: Boxed warning: can cause injury and death to an unborn baby, so it must be stopped when pregnancy is detected. Food reduces how much captopril is absorbed, so it is taken 1 hour before meals (or 2 hours after). Blood counts and kidney function may be checked, especially in kidney or autoimmune disease. Taste changes usually improve within about 8 to 12 weeks, even with continued use. Do not use with sacubitril/valsartan, and avoid aliskiren in people with diabetes or kidney impairment. Potassium supplements, salt substitutes and NSAIDs can interact.
olderAdultSafety: The 2023 AGS Beers Criteria recommends avoiding routine use of this medicine together with another renin-angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitor, and avoiding routine use with a potassium-sparing diuretic in older adults with chronic kidney disease Stage 3a or higher, because of the risk of high potassium and kidney injury. Combining it with lithium should generally be avoided or require close monitoring of lithium levels. Drug references advise a lower starting dose in older adults because kidney function declines with age. Older adults are also more prone to dizziness, low blood pressure and falls, so regular blood tests are needed to monitor kidney function and potassium levels.
caregiverGuidance: Give 1 hour before meals (or 2 hours after) at the same times each day, even if the older adult feels well. Do not double a missed dose. Do not stop it without asking the doctor. Keep scheduled blood tests. Do not give potassium supplements or potassium-based salt substitutes unless the doctor approves. Ask the doctor or pharmacist before giving ibuprofen or similar pain relievers, or the antibiotic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, because they can affect the kidneys or raise potassium with this medicine. Help the older adult stand up slowly. Report fever, sore throat, mouth sores, rash, a persistent dry cough, loss of taste, or reduced urine. Do not confuse captopril with carvedilol. Seek emergency help for swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, or difficulty breathing.

name: Carvedilol
drugClass: Nonselective beta-blocker with alpha-1 blocking activity (alpha/beta-adrenergic blocker)
usedFor: Treats chronic heart failure and high blood pressure, and reduces the risk of death after a heart attack in people with reduced heart function.
howItWorks: Blocks beta receptors and alpha-1 receptors. This slows the heart rate and widens blood vessels, which lowers blood pressure and reduces the heart's workload.
adverseEffects: Worsening heart failure or fluid retention
Wheezing in people with lung disease
Chest pain or heart attack if stopped suddenly
Can hide the signs of low blood sugar
Severe allergic or skin reaction (such as angioedema or Stevens-Johnson syndrome)
warnings: Take with food to slow absorption and reduce dizziness when standing. Do not stop it suddenly, because coronary artery disease can suddenly worsen. It should not be used in asthma or related bronchospasm, second- or third-degree heart block, sick sinus syndrome, severe slow heartbeat, or severe liver impairment. It can cause intraoperative floppy iris syndrome during cataract surgery, so the eye surgeon should be told. It can strengthen the effect of insulin and diabetes medicines.
olderAdultSafety: Carvedilol is not named individually in the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria. Because it also blocks alpha receptors, older adults are more prone to low blood pressure on standing, dizziness and falls, especially after a dose increase or when taken with diuretics or other blood pressure medicines. In heart failure the label starts at a low dose (3.125 mg twice daily) and raises it slowly.
caregiverGuidance: Give with food, at the same times each day (twice daily for regular tablets). Never stop it suddenly or let the supply run out. Check pulse and blood pressure as the doctor directs, and ask which pulse number means the dose should be held and the doctor called. Help the older adult stand up slowly. If the older adult has heart failure, weigh them at the same time each day and record it. Report fainting, a very slow pulse, new shortness of breath, leg swelling, rapid weight gain, or wheezing. Do not confuse carvedilol with captopril. Seek emergency help for chest pain or severe trouble breathing.
sources: DailyMed and Drugs@FDA (Coreg and carvedilol tablets labels)

name: Cilazapril
usedFor: Treats high blood pressure and chronic heart failure. Cilazapril is sold in countries such as Ireland, Canada and New Zealand under names like Vascace, Inhibace and Zapril; it is not available in the US.
howItWorks: Blocks an enzyme that makes angiotensin II, a substance that tightens blood vessels. The blood vessels relax and widen, which lowers blood pressure. Cilazapril is converted in the body to the active form, cilazaprilat.
adverseEffects: Angioedema (swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat)
Low blood pressure with dizziness or fainting
warnings: Should not be used with a history of angioedema from an ACE inhibitor, or with sacubitril/valsartan. Low blood pressure can occur after the first dose, especially in people with heart failure, on diuretics, or who are dehydrated. Use caution in kidney disease; doses are lowered when creatinine clearance is reduced (for example, 0.5 mg starting dose when clearance is 10 to 40 mL/min). Should not be started in pregnancy.
olderAdultSafety: Product information for cilazapril advises starting at a low dose in older adults (0.5 to 1 mg once daily for high blood pressure, and strictly 0.5 mg for heart failure), because older adults can have higher blood levels of the active form and are more sensitive to blood pressure drops. name: Cilnidipine
drugClass: Calcium channel blocker (dihydropyridine; blocks L-type and N-type calcium channels)
usedFor: Treats high blood pressure. Cilnidipine is used in countries such as Japan, India and Bangladesh; it is not FDA-approved in the US.
howItWorks: Blocks calcium from entering the muscle cells of blood vessels, so the vessels relax and widen. It also blocks N-type calcium channels on sympathetic nerve endings, which reduces the release of norepinephrine, a chemical that can raise blood pressure and heart rate.
adverseEffects: Worsening chest pain or heart attack signs
Liver problems (yellowing of the skin or eyes, rare)
warnings: Use with caution in people with severe liver impairment or a history of serious reactions to calcium channel blockers. Sudden withdrawal of a calcium channel blocker can worsen symptoms, so the dose should be lowered gradually under medical supervision. Some product labels list cardiogenic shock, recent heart attack, unstable angina and severe aortic stenosis as reasons not to use it. Dizziness from the blood pressure drop can affect driving and activities needing alertness.
olderAdultSafety: Cilnidipine is not named in the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria. Product information advises giving it carefully under close observation in older adults, starting with a low dose (for example, 5 mg), because older adults are more sensitive to blood pressure drops and excessive lowering should be avoided. Watch for dizziness, fainting and falls.
caregiverGuidance: Give once daily as directed on the product label, at the same time each day. Check blood pressure regularly and help the older adult stand up slowly. Look at the ankles for swelling. Do not stop it suddenly without asking the doctor. Report fainting, chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat, or yellowing of the skin or eyes. Seek emergency help for chest pain that does not go away or fainting.
sources: Siddiqui et al., AKMMC Journal 2019 (review of new-generation calcium channel blockers)

name: Clonidine
drugClass: Central alpha-2 adrenergic agonist (centrally acting antihypertensive)
usedFor: Treats high blood pressure (regular tablets). Extended-release clonidine tablets and patches are used for other conditions such as ADHD.
howItWorks: Stimulates alpha-2 receptors in the brain stem, which reduces the nerve signals that tighten blood vessels and speed up the heart. Blood pressure and heart rate fall.
adverseEffects: Rebound high blood pressure if stopped suddenly (headache, nervousness, racing heartbeat, and in serious cases stroke)
warnings: Do not stop it suddenly; the dose must be tapered gradually (over several days) to avoid rebound hypertension, especially at higher doses or when taken with a beta-blocker. It can cause drowsiness, so avoid alcohol and other sedating medicines. Use caution in kidney impairment (lower starting dose and slow increases), in people with a slow heartbeat or heart block, and in those prone to fainting or dehydration.
olderAdultSafety: The 2023 AGS Beers Criteria recommends avoiding clonidine as first-line treatment for high blood pressure, and avoiding other central alpha-agonists, because of the high risk of adverse central nervous system effects (such as drowsiness and confusion), slow heart rate and low blood pressure on standing. If an older adult is already taking it, it should not be stopped suddenly; the doctor should review whether a safer medicine is suitable.
caregiverGuidance: Never stop it suddenly or let the supply run out, because blood pressure can rise dangerously. Give at the same times each day; if the doctor prescribed a larger dose at bedtime, follow that, since it can reduce daytime drowsiness. Check blood pressure and pulse as directed. Watch for confusion, excessive sleepiness, constipation and falls, and help the older adult stand up slowly. Ask the doctor about safer options. Seek emergency help for fainting, a severe headache with very high blood pressure after missed doses, or a very slow heartbeat.

name: Diltiazem Hydrochloride
usedFor: Treats high blood pressure (extended-release forms), chronic stable angina (chest pain), and angina caused by coronary artery spasm.
howItWorks: Blocks calcium from entering heart and blood vessel muscle cells. This relaxes blood vessels, lowers blood pressure, slows the heart rate and reduces the heart's workload.
commonSideEffects: Swelling of the ankles or legs
adverseEffects: Heart block (first-degree AV block is common, second- or third-degree is rare)
Liver injury (yellowing of the skin or eyes, rare)
warnings: Should not be used in sick sinus syndrome or second- or third-degree heart block (unless a pacemaker is in place), with low blood pressure (below 90 systolic), or with acute heart attack and fluid in the lungs. Diltiazem raises levels of several medicines (CYP3A4 effect), including some statins such as simvastatin and atorvastatin (higher risk of muscle damage), some sedatives and cyclosporine. Combining with beta-blockers can cause a dangerously slow heart rate or heart block. Grapefruit juice may increase diltiazem levels.
olderAdultSafety: The 2023 AGS Beers Criteria recommends avoiding non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as diltiazem in older adults with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), because they can worsen heart failure. Product information also notes that blood levels of diltiazem may be higher in older adults and in those with kidney or liver impairment, so heart rate should be monitored closely, especially at the start of treatment.
caregiverGuidance: Swallow extended-release capsules and tablets whole; do not crush or chew them. Check pulse and blood pressure as the doctor directs, and ask which pulse number means the dose should be held and the doctor called. Avoid grapefruit juice. Check with the pharmacist before adding any new medicine, especially cholesterol medicines, sedatives and other heart medicines. Report ankle swelling, new shortness of breath, fainting, or a very slow pulse. Seek emergency help for fainting, chest pain that does not go away, or severe trouble breathing.
sources: Health Products Regulatory Authority, Ireland (diltiazem SmPCs)

name: Enalapril
usedFor: Treats high blood pressure and heart failure, and helps prevent heart failure in people whose heart pumps less strongly but who do not yet have symptoms.
howItWorks: Blocks an enzyme that makes angiotensin II, a substance that tightens blood vessels. The blood vessels relax and widen, which lowers blood pressure. Enalapril is a prodrug that the liver converts to the active form, enalaprilat.
adverseEffects: Angioedema (swelling of the face, lips, tongue, throat or limbs)
Liver problems (yellowing of the skin or eyes)
Low white blood cell count (fever, sore throat)
warnings: Boxed warning: can cause injury and death to an unborn baby, so it must be stopped when pregnancy is detected. Use with caution in kidney disease, dehydration, heart failure, or when taking diuretics; the dose is lowered in kidney impairment. Do not use with sacubitril/valsartan, or within 36 hours of switching to or from it. Avoid aliskiren in people with diabetes. Potassium supplements, potassium-based salt substitutes and NSAIDs can interact. A history of angioedema is a reason not to use it.
olderAdultSafety: The 2023 AGS Beers Criteria recommends avoiding routine use of this medicine together with another renin-angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitor, and avoiding routine use with a potassium-sparing diuretic in older adults with chronic kidney disease Stage 3a or higher, because of the risk of high potassium and kidney injury. Combining it with lithium should generally be avoided or require close monitoring of lithium levels. Older adults are also more prone to dizziness, low blood pressure and falls, so regular blood tests are needed to monitor kidney function and potassium levels.

Do not give potassium supplements or potassium-based salt substitutes unless the doctor approves. Seek emergency help for swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, or difficulty breathing.

name: Eplerenone
drugClass: Aldosterone receptor antagonist (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist); potassium-sparing diuretic
usedFor: Treats high blood pressure and heart failure after a heart attack (to reduce the risk of death in people with reduced heart function).
howItWorks: Blocks aldosterone, a hormone that makes the body hold on to salt and water. The body removes more salt and water but keeps potassium, which lowers blood pressure and eases the strain on the heart.
commonSideEffects: Breast tenderness or enlargement in men
adverseEffects: Dangerously high potassium (weakness or heavy legs, tingling, irregular heartbeat, confusion)
warnings: Potassium and kidney function must be checked before and during treatment. It should not be used if serum potassium is above 5.5 mEq/L at the start, if creatinine clearance is 30 mL/min or lower, or with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (such as ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin or ritonavir). For high blood pressure it is also not used in type 2 diabetes with microalbuminuria or with raised serum creatinine. ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium supplements, other potassium-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs and lithium can raise potassium or affect the kidneys. Grapefruit juice raises eplerenone levels.
olderAdultSafety: Eplerenone is not named individually in the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria. However, because it is a potassium-sparing diuretic, the Beers caution against routinely combining a potassium-sparing diuretic with an ACE inhibitor or ARB in older adults with chronic kidney disease Stage 3a or higher (risk of high potassium) is relevant. The FDA label reports no substantial differences in safety or effectiveness between older and younger adults, but older adults are more likely to have age-related kidney problems, which raises the risk of high potassium. Regular blood tests for kidney function and potassium are important.
caregiverGuidance: Give at the same time each day, with or without food. Keep every blood test for potassium and kidney function. Do not give potassium supplements or potassium-based salt substitutes unless the doctor approves, and avoid grapefruit juice. Check with the pharmacist before adding any antibiotic, antifungal, or pain reliever such as ibuprofen. Report muscle weakness, an irregular heartbeat, very little urine, or confusion promptly. Seek emergency help for severe weakness, fainting, or a very slow or irregular heartbeat.

name: Eprosartan
usedFor: Treats high blood pressure (hypertension), alone or with other blood pressure medicines. The Teveten brand has been discontinued in the US, but generic eprosartan may be available.
howItWorks: Blocks angiotensin II, a substance that narrows blood vessels, from acting on the blood vessels. The vessels relax, which lowers blood pressure.
adverseEffects: Swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat (angioedema)
Severe low blood pressure or fainting, especially in older adults and in people who are dehydrated
warnings: Boxed warning: can cause injury and death to an unborn baby, so it must be stopped when pregnancy is detected. Low blood pressure is more likely with dehydration or salt depletion. Kidney function and potassium should be monitored. Avoid combining with ACE inhibitors or aliskiren, since the combination raises the risk of low blood pressure, kidney problems and high potassium. Lithium levels may rise.
olderAdultSafety: The Health Canada product monograph states that eprosartan was well tolerated and effective in older adults with high blood pressure, but that appropriate caution should be used because increased vulnerability to drug effect is possible. The 2023 AGS Beers Criteria recommends avoiding routine use of this medicine together with another renin-angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitor, and avoiding routine use with a potassium-sparing diuretic in older adults with chronic kidney disease Stage 3a or higher, because of the risk of high potassium and kidney injury. Older adults are also more prone to dizziness, low blood pressure and falls, so regular blood tests are needed to monitor kidney function and potassium levels.

Ask the doctor or pharmacist before giving ibuprofen or similar pain relievers, or the antibiotic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, because they can affect the kidneys or raise potassium with this medicine. Help the older adult stand up slowly. Call the doctor for vomiting, diarrhea or poor drinking. Report dizziness, fainting, or reduced urine. Seek emergency help for swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, or difficulty breathing.

name: Esmolol
usedFor: Used to slow a heartbeat that is too fast, and to keep heart rate and blood pressure from spiking during or right after surgery.
howItWorks: Slows the heart by blocking the body's "speed up" signals. It works quickly and wears off quickly, so the care team canadjust it easily. At higher does it can also affect the lungs and blood vessels.
warnings: This medicine is given only in the hospital through IV. It can cause very low blood pressure, a slow heartbeat and worsenin heart failure. It should not be used in older adults with very slow heartbeat, heart block or severe heart failure.
olderAdultSafety: Olde adults are more sensitive to low blood pressure and a slow pulse, so their heart rate and blood pressure should be monitored continuously during treatment. Dizziness and confusion can raise the risk of falls once the person is up and moving.
caregiverGuidance: Since this medicine is administered by healthcare professionals, caregivers should observe the older adult and promptly report any changes. Inform the nurse about dizziness, fainting, chest pain, difficulty breathing, confusion, or pain and swelling at the IV site. Before discharge, ask the doctor whether any changes were made to the heart medication regimen and what monitoring is needed at home.

name: Felodipine
usedFor: Used to lower high blood pressure. It may be used alone or with other medicines for high blood pressure.
howItWorks: Relaxes and widens the blood vessels. This allow blood to flow more easily, which helps lower high blood pressure. May sometimes cause a slight increase in heart rate.
warnings: This medicine commonly causs ankle sweling, flushing, headache, and swollen gums. It may worsen chest pain when first started or when dose is increased. Grapefruit juice may increase the medicine's effecr and risk of side effects.
olderAdultSafety: Older adults are more likely to experience dizziness, swelling, and falls, so doctors usually start with a low dose. New or worsening swelling should be assessed by a healthcare professional, as it may indicate an underlying heart problem, including heart failure.

Check blood pressure and pulse regularly, and help the older adult stand up slowly. Seek emergency medical care if fainting, chest pain, shortness of breath or sudden leg swelling occurs.

name: Fimasartan
usedFor: Treatment of high blood pressure and heart failure.
howItWorks: Blocks the signal that makes the blood vessels tighten and makes the body retain salt and water. This relaxes the blood vessel and reduces blood volume, resulting in lower blood pressure.
warnings: This medicine can raise potassium levels, harm the kidneys and lower blood pressure too much, especially when the person is dehydrated. Swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat is an emergency.

Follow the prescribed fluid intake, especially during vomiting, diarrhea, or hot weather. Monitor blood pressure regularly. Report dizziness, fainting, reduced urine output, or muscle weakness to the doctor. Seek emergency medical care for swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat.

name: Furosemide
usedFor: A "water pill" that helps the body get rid of excess salt and water through urine. This helps reduce swelling/fluid retention and can also help lower blood pressure.
howItWorks: Blocks the kidney from taking back too much salt. So the salt stays in the urine, and water follows the salt.
commonSideEffects: Pain, itching, swelling or redness at injection site (for injectable forms)
adverseEffects: Severe hypotension with dehydration and worsening kidney function
warnings: This medicine may cause dehydration, low sodium and potassium levels, low blood pressure, and increased urination. High doses may affect hearing. Use with caution in older adults wit kidney disease or gout.
olderAdultSafety: The 2023 AGS Beers Criteria recommends caution with diuretics because they can cause low sodium levels. Sodium levels should be checked soon after starting furosemide or changing its dose. In older women, avoid combining furosemide with alpha-1 blockers such as doxazosin, prazosin, or terazosin because this may increase the risk of urinary incontinence. Furosemide may also increase lithium levels, so lithium levels should be closely monitored when the medicines are used together.
caregiverGuidance: Give the medicine in the morning, or as directed, to reduce nighttime trips to the bathroom. Keep the path to the toilet clear and use a night light or bedside commode if needed to prevent falls. If the older adult has heart failure, monitor and record their weight daily. Report confusion, leg cramps, extreme thirst, dizziness, or very little urine to the doctor. Seek immediate medical attention for fainting, rapid weight gain, or ringing in the ears, especially after high doses.

name: Hydralazine
usedFor: Used to treat high blood pressure.
howItWorks: Relaxes and widens the blood vessels. This makes it easier for blood to flow, so the pressure inside the blood vessels goes down.
warnings: This medicine may cause headaches, a rapid heartbeat, and fluid retention. Long-term use at higher doses may cause a lupus-like reaction, which can include joint pain, fever, and rash. Use caution in older adults with coronary artery disease, as the medicine may increase the heart's workload.
olderAdultSafety: Older adults are more susceptible to low blood pressure, dizziness, and falls, so the dose should be increased gradually under medical supervision. A rapid heartbeat may also trigger chest pain in older adults with heart disease.
caregiverGuidance: Give the medicine consistently each day, either with food or on an empty stomach, as directed. Check the older adult’s pulse and blood pressure regularly, and help them rise slowly from a bed or chair to prevent dizziness and falls. Contact the doctor if joint pain, fever, rash, chest pain, a racing heartbeat, or leg swelling occurs. Seek emergency medical care for severe chest pain or difficulty breathing.

usedFor: Used to lower high blood pressure and remove excess water from the body.
howItWorks: Makes the kidneys remove more salt and water from the body through urine. Reduces reabsorption of sodium and chloride.

Contact the doctor for confusion, weakness, muscle cramps, or dizziness. Seek urgent medical care for fainting or eye pain, especially if accompanied by sudden vision changes.

name: Hydroflumethiazide

name: Imidapril
usedFor: Used to lower high blood pressure

name: Isosorbide dinitrate
usedFor: Preventin of chest pain caused by coronary artery disease.
howItWorks: Relaxes the blood vessels, especially the veins, reducing the amount of blood returning to the heart and decreasing the heart's workload.
warnings: This medicine commonly causes headaches, flushing, and dizziness. Never combine it with sildenafil, tadalafil, or similar medicines, as this can cause a dangerous drop in blood pressure. Do not stop taking it suddenly without medical advice.
olderAdultSafety: Older adults are more susceptible to dizziness, fainting, and falls, particularly when standing up or shortly after taking a dose. Treatment should start at a low dose and be adjusted carefully under medical supervision.
caregiverGuidance: Give each dose at the times prescribed by the doctor. Do not crush or chew extended-release tablets. If the older adult feels dizzy, have them sit or lie down and help them stand slowly. Ensure they do not take sildenafil, tadalafil, or similar medicines with this treatment. Seek emergency medical care for fainting or chest pain that does not go away.

name: Ivabradine (as HCL)
usedFor: Used to reduce the risk of hospitalization due to worsening chronic heart failure.
howItWorks: Slows the heart rate by acting on the pacemaker cells of the heart without reducing the heart's pumping strength.
commonSideEffects: Temporary visual brightness or flashing lights
adverseEffects: Very fast heartbeat from the lower chambers of the heart (ventricular tachycardia)
Chaotic heartbeat that prevents proper pumping (ventricular fibrillation)
Dangerous abnormal heart rhythm (torsade de pointes)
Swelling of the face, lips, tongue and throat
warnings: This medicine may cause a very slow heartbeat, an irregular heart rhythm such as atrial fibrillation, and temporary flashes of light in the field of vision. Grapefruit juice and certain antibiotics and antifungal medicines can increase the amount of the medicine in the body, raising the risk of side effects.
olderAdultSafety: Older adults may be more susceptible to a slow heart rate and dizziness. Heart rate should be checked regularly, and the doctor may adjust the dose if it becomes too slow.

Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice, and consult the doctor or pharmacist before starting any new medicine and check for any drug interaction. name: Labetalol
drugClass: Beta-Blockers- Combined Alpha and Beta-Receptor Blockers
usedFor: Used to quickly lower very high blood pressure (severe hypertension), especially in hospitalized patients.
howItWorks: Relaxes the blood vessels and slows the heart, causing blood pressure to decrease.
commonSideEffects: Tingling of the scalp or skin
adverseEffects: Yellowing of the skin or eyes
Severe allergic reaction with swelling and difficulty breathing
Difficulty breathing due to airway narrowing
warnings: Labetalol may cause low blood pressure, dizziness, and a slow heartbeat. Rarely, it may cause liver problems. It can mask some warning signs of low blood sugar and may worsen asthma or other conditions involving airway narrowing. It should not be stopped abruptly without medical advice.
olderAdultSafety: Older adults are more susceptible to low blood pressure, dizziness, and falls. IV labetalol requires careful monitoring of blood pressure and heart rate during and after administration. The dose should be adjusted according to the patient’s response.
caregiverGuidance: Since labetalol is administered by a healthcare professional, caregivers should report dizziness, weakness, wheezing, or unusual changes in alertness immediately. Help the older adult change positions slowly once permitted. Inform the healthcare team of any history of asthma, diabetes, or liver disease. Report yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or an unusually slow heartbeat promptly. Seek emergency medical attention for fainting, severe breathing difficulty, or signs of dangerously low blood pressure.

name: Lacidipine
usedFor: Used to lower high blood presure. It can be used alone or with other antihypertensive medicines.
howItWorks: Blocks calcium from entering the muscles of blood vessels, causing blood vessels to relax and widen, which owers blood pressure.
adverseEffects: Swelling of the face, lips, mouth or throat
warnings: This medicine may cause dizziness, headache, flushing, ankle swelling, and a fast or uneven heartbeat. Use caution in patients with an uneven heartbeat, other heart problems, or liver problems. Lacidipine may cause chest pain, particularly when treatment is first started, and may lower blood pressure too much. Patients should also inform their healthcare provider about other medicines they are taking, especially other antihypertensives, rifampicin, itraconazole, cyclosporin, cimetidine, and corticosteroids. Grapefruit juice should be avoided because it may affect the action of lacidipine.

Seek emergency medical care if the patient develops chest pain, fainting, or rapid swelling of the face, mouth, or throat with difficulty breathing.

name: Lercanidipine
usedFor: Used to treat mild to moderate high blood pressure (essential hypertension) in adults.

commonSideEffects: Swelling of the ankles or legs
adverseEffects: Swelling of the face, lips, or throat
In older adults on peritoneal dialysis, cloudy dialysis fluid (peritoneal cloudy effluent)
warnings: This medicine may cause headache, dizziness, flushing, palpitations, ankle swelling, and low blood pressure. Avoid grapefruit juice and alcohol. Use with caution in patients with heart problems, mild to moderate liver or kidney disease, or sick sinus syndrome without a pacemaker. Avoid use with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors and cyclosporine. Severe liver or kidney disease is a contraindication.
olderAdultSafety: No routine dose adjustment is required based on age alone, but treatment should be started carefully in older adults. Monitor for dizziness, low blood pressure, fainting, and falls. Use caution with liver or kidney problems, especially because severe impairment is a contraindication.
caregiverGuidance: Give in the morning at least 15 minutes before breakfast, at the same time each day. Do not give grapefruit juice or alcohol. Monitor blood pressure, dizziness, fainting, ankle swelling, and chest pain. Help the patient stand slowly to prevent falls. Report severe chest pain, fainting, difficulty breathing, or unusual swelling.

name: Levamlodipine (as besilate)
usedFor: Used to lower high blood pressure in adults. It may used alone or with other hypertensive medicines.

name: Lisinopril
usedFor: Treat high blood pressure (hypertension)
howItWorks: Works by blocking a substance in the body that causes the blood vessels to tighten. It relaxes the blood vessels. This lowers blood pressure and increases the supply of blood and oxygen to the heart.
commonSideEffects: Decrease in urine output or decrease in urine-concentrating ability
Faintness or lightheadedness when getting up suddenly from a lying or sitting position
adverseEffects: Swelling of the face, lips, tongue, throat or limbs (angioedema)
Hoarseness or trouble breathing or swallowing
Fever, sore throat or chills (signs of infection)
Yellowing of the skin or eyes
warnings: Extra caution is needed for people with kidney problems, dehydration, low blood pressure or high potassium. Do not use with sacubitril/valsartan, and avoid use with aliskiren in people with diabetes. Aspirin, NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen), potassium supplements and potassium-based salt substitutes can interact. Vomiting, diarrhea or heavy sweating can lower blood pressure.
olderAdultSafety: Older adults may be more sensitive to low blood pressure and may have reduced kidney function. Taking it together with another blood pressure medicine of this type (an ARB, ARNI or aliskiren) or a potassium-sparing water pill can raise potassium to unsafe levels, especially with kidney disease. Blood tests may be needed to check kidney function and potassium levels.
caregiverGuidance: Help the older adult take the medicine once daily at about the same time. Do not stop it without asking the doctor, even if they feel well. Keep blood pressure checks and scheduled blood tests. Do not give potassium supplements or potassium-based salt substitutes unless the healthcare provider approves. If the person feels dizzy, help them sit down and rise slowly. If a dose is missed, give it when remembered unless the next dose is near; never double up. Seek emergency help for swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, or difficulty breathing.

name: Losartan
usedFor: Treatment of hypertension (high blood pressure); lowering stroke risk in people with hypertension and an enlarged heart; and protecting the kidneys in type 2 diabetes with hypertension.

adverseEffects: Swelling of the face, lips, tongue, throat or limbs (angioedema)
warnings: Extra caution is needed for people with kidney or liver problems, heart failure or dehydration. Avoid use with aliskiren in people with diabetes. name: Losartan (as Potassium)
usedFor: Treatment of hypertension; lowering stroke risk in people with hypertension and an enlarged left heart; kidney protection in type 2 diabetes with hypertension
howItWorks: Blocks substances that tighten blood vessels, so blood vessels relax and blood pressure drops.
adverseEffects: Swelling of the face, throat, tongue, lips or limbs
warnings: Dizziness or fainting is most likely when starting, or when they stand up quickly. Vomiting, diarrhea or poor drinking can make it worse, so call the doctor. Don’t give ibuprofen, naproxen or potassium products unless approved. Kidney and potassium blood tests are needed. Tell the doctor about liver problems, since a lower starting dose may be needed.
olderAdultSafety: The label found no overall differences in safety or effectiveness between older and younger patients, but some older people may be more sensitive. Watch for dizziness and falls, and keep blood pressure checks.
caregiverGuidance: Give at the same times daily; full effect takes 3 to 6 weeks. Don’t stop it or double a missed dose. Avoid potassium products and NSAIDs unless approved. Have them rest their feet on the floor before standing, and call the doctor about vomiting or diarrhea. Emergency: facial or throat swelling.

name: Manidipine
usedFor: Treatment of mild to moderate hypertension.
howItWorks: Relaxes blood vessels with little effect on heart pumping, which lowers blood pressure.
warnings: Dizziness and low blood pressure can lead to falls, so check blood pressure regularly if the doctor asked. Don’t give grapefruit juice. Ask the pharmacist before adding antifungals or antibiotics. Tell the doctor about liver or kidney problems, or heart problems such as unstable angina.
olderAdultSafety: Once-daily manidipine as effective and generally well tolerated in younger and elderly adults with mild to moderate hypertension. It was also effective in patients with type 2 diabetes or kidney impairment, with less ankle swelling than amlodipine in a large trial.
caregiverGuidance: Give once daily, usually in the morning. No grapefruit juice. Help them rise slowly and watch for ankle swelling. Check with the pharmacist before adding antifungals or antibiotics. Emergency: fainting or chest pain

name: Mannitol
usedFor: Reducing pressure inside the skull (and brain swelling) and elevated pressure inside the eye. Given by IV.
howItWorks: Draws water from tissues into the blood, and the kidneys remove the extra water as urine.
adverseEffects: Fluid overload, heart failure or lung fluid
Low or high sodium and potassium
Pain or swelling at the IV site
warnings: Given by IV by hospital staff, not at home. Staff check kidney, heart, lung and fluid status first. Your role is to tell the nurse about confusion, unusual sleepiness, shortness of breath, swelling, little urine, or IV-site pain. Bring a current medicine list, because water pills and some other drugs raise kidney risk.
olderAdultSafety: Mannitol is cleared mainly by the kidneys, so adverse reactions may be greater in elderly patients with impaired kidney function. Check kidney, heart and lung status first and correct fluid and electrolyte problems before giving it.
caregiverGuidance: Given by IV by staff, not at home. Stay with them and tell the nurse about confusion, unusual sleepiness, shortness of breath, swelling, little urine, or IV-site pain or swelling. Bring a current medicine list.

name: Meformin hydrochloride
usedFor: Control of blood sugar in adults and children 10 and older with type 2 diabetes, with diet and exercise.
howItWorks: Reduces sugar made by the liver and absorbed from food, and improves the body’s response to insulin.
adverseEffects: Lactic acidosis (weakness, muscle pain, trouble breathing, unusual sleepiness, stomach pain, nausea or vomiting, feeling cold, dizziness, slow or irregular heartbeat)
Low blood sugar when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas
warnings: Rare but serious lactic acidosis is more likely at 65 and older, with kidney trouble, dehydration or heavy alcohol use. Keep kidney blood tests, at least yearly. On sick days with vomiting, severe diarrhea, fever or poor drinking, call the doctor the same day, since it may need pausing. Tell the doctor before surgery or X-ray dye tests. Seek emergency help for fast breathing, severe weakness, stomach pain or unusual sleepiness.
olderAdultSafety: The label advises starting at a low dose in older adults and checking kidney function more often, because kidney function declines with age.
caregiverGuidance: Give with meals; swallow extended-release tablets whole. Check blood sugar and keep kidney tests. Call the doctor the same day for vomiting, severe diarrhea, fever or poor drinking, and before surgery or X-ray dye. Emergency: fast breathing, severe weakness, stomach pain or unusual sleepiness.

name: Methyldopa
usedFor: Treatment of hypertension.

name: Metoprolol
usedFor: It treats high blood pressure, angina (chest pain), and heart failure. It also improves survival after a heart attack and is sometimes used for irregular heartbeats.
howItWorks: It blocks beta-1 receptors in the heart, so the heart beats more slowly and with less force. This lowers blood pressure and the heart’s workload.
commonSideEffects: Tiredness, dizziness, a slow pulse, cold hands and feet, and low blood pressure are the most common

The older adult should stand up slowly to avoid falls.
olderAdultSafety: For metoprolol, the main older adult concerns are a pulse that becomes too slow, dizziness on standing, tiredness, and falls. caregiverGuidance: Keep a daily record of pulse and blood pressure. Give doses at the same times each day, and refill early so the medicine never runs out. Call the doctor for fainting, a very slow pulse, new shortness of breath, leg swelling, or fast weight gain.

name: Nifedipine
usedFor: It treats high blood pressure and angina. It is also sometimes used for preterm labor and Raynaud’s syndrome. It comes as a capsule and as an extended-release tablet.
howItWorks: It relaxes blood vessels so the heart does not have to pump as hard, and it improves blood and oxygen supply to the heart.

name: Nimodipine
usedFor: It reduces brain damage after a subarachnoid hemorrhage, which is bleeding in the space around the brain. It is not a routine blood pressure medicine. Treatment should begin as soon as possible, no later than 96 hours after the bleed.
howItWorks: It relaxes blood vessels in the brain, allowing more blood to reach damaged areas.
commonSideEffects: Low blood pressure, headache, flushing, and nausea are the most common
adverseEffects: The main serious effect is a significant drop in blood pressure. Heartbeat changes and swelling can also occur
warnings: It must never be given into a vein, because this can cause life-threatening effects or death. If the capsule contents must be given through a feeding tube, only an oral syringe should be used, as the care team instructs. Grapefruit and grapefruit juice should be avoided. The full course should be completed, and the doctor will watch blood pressure closely.
olderAdultSafety: Older adults recovering from a brain bleed are often frail, so the main concern is a fall in blood pressure causing dizziness, fainting, and falls. Blood pressure is monitored carefully during treatment. Check blood pressure and avoiding unnecessary extra blood-pressure-lowering drugs. At home, the older adult should have help when getting up, and any new confusion or drowsiness should be reported right away.
caregiverGuidance: Follow the exact schedule and duration the doctor gave. Label any oral syringe “Not for IV use” if one is used. Report fainting, severe dizziness, a worsening headache, or new confusion right away.

name: Nitrogylcerin
usedFor: It treats episodes of angina in people with coronary artery disease. Sublingual tablets are taken under the tongue as needed and can also be used just before activities that trigger angina. Patches, ointment, and sprays also exist.

Because chest pain can be a medical emergency, older adults should also have a written plan and know when to call for help.

name: Olmesartan
usedFor: It treats high blood pressure and is often combined with amlodipine or a water pill
howItWorks: It blocks angiotensin II from binding to its receptors, so blood vessels relax and blood pressure falls.
commonSideEffects: Dizziness is the main common effect and is more likely when treatment starts

caregiverGuidance: Give it at the same time each day, even when the person feels well. Keep lab appointments. Report face or lip swelling, persistent diarrhea, very little urine, or fainting right away.

name: Perindopril
usedFor: Treats high blood pressure. Lowers the risk of heart attack and heart-related death in people with stable coronary artery disease.

warnings: Use cautiously in patients with kidney or liver impairment, heart failure, dehydration, or diabetes. Monitor blood pressure, kidney function, and potassium levels. Avoid potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics, and NSAIDs unless approved by the doctor. Contraindicated during pregnancy and in patients with a history of ACE inhibitor-related angioedema.

Inform all healthcare providers about the medication and seek emergency help for facial or throat swelling or difficulty breathing.

name: Sodium Nitroprusside
usedFor: Rapidly lowers dangerously high blood pressure, treats acute heart failure in selected patients, and produces controlled low blood pressure during surgery.
howItWorks: Relaxes blood vessels, causing arteries and veins to widen. This lowers blood pressure and reduces the workload of the heart.
commonSideEffects: Nausea, dizziness, headache, sweating, and palpitations

warnings: Administer only as a controlled IV infusion using an infusion pump. Continuously monitor blood pressure and assess acid-base balance and signs of toxicity. name: Spironolactone
usedFor: Helps manage heart failure, high blood pressure, and swelling caused by fluid buildup. This lowers blood pressure and reduces swelling.
howItWorks: Helps remove excess salt and water through urine while keeping potassium in the body.
commonSideEffects: Stomach upset, leg cramps, dizziness, tiredness, and breast swelling or soreness (in men and women). Lowered sexual desire or erection problems and hair thinning may also occur
adverseEffects: High potassium (weakness or heavy legs, tingling, irregular heartbeat, confusion), kidney problems, dehydration or very low blood pressure, severe allergic reaction (swelling of the face, lips, or tongue), and yellow skin or eyes
warnings: Use with caution in people with kidney problems or high potassium levels. Avoid potassium supplements and salt substitutes containing potassium unless prescribed.
olderAdultSafety: Older adults are more likely to have reduced kidney function and may be more sensitive to low blood pressure and dizziness. Regular blood tests for kidney function and potassium are important.
caregiverGuidance: Help the older adult take the medicine as prescribed and attend scheduled blood tests. Help them sit down if dizzy. Report muscle weakness, irregular heartbeat, very little urine, or confusion promptly. Seek emergency help for severe symptoms.

name: Tadalafil
usedFor: Treats erectile dysfunction (ED), symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), and, in specific formulations, pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH).
howItWorks: Inhibits the PDE5 enzyme, increasing cGMP levels and relaxing smooth muscles in blood vessels. This improves blood flow and, depending on the indication, helps achieve an erection, relieve urinary symptoms, or lower pressure in pulmonary arteries.
commonSideEffects: Headache, indigestion, back pain, muscle aches, flushing, and nasal congestion
adverseEffects: Severe hypotension, prolonged erection lasting over 4 hours (priapism), sudden vision or hearing loss, and serious cardiovascular events in susceptible patients
warnings: Must not be taken with nitrates (e.g., nitroglycerin) or riociguat because of the risk of severe hypotension. Use cautiously with alpha-blockers, antihypertensives, and alcohol. Dose adjustment may be needed in kidney or liver impairment. Seek urgent care for chest pain, sudden vision or hearing loss, or an erection lasting over 4 hours.
olderAdultSafety: Older adults may be more vulnerable to dizziness and low blood pressure, particularly when taking other antihypertensives. Review kidney and liver function and the patient's medication list before treatment.
caregiverGuidance: Administer only as prescribed and check for possible interactions with other medicines. Assist with position changes if dizziness occurs. Teach the patient not to use nitrates while taking tadalafil and to seek emergency care for chest pain, sudden vision or hearing changes, or a prolonged erection.

name: Telmisartan

howItWorks: Blocks angiotensin II from tightening blood vessels, allowing them to relax and lowering blood pressure.
adverseEffects: Severe hypotension, hyperkalemia, kidney impairment, and fetal harm during pregnancy
warnings: Monitor blood pressure, kidney function, and potassium levels. Use cautiously in dehydration, kidney or liver impairment. Avoid potassium supplements and salt substitutes unless approved. Avoid combining with ACE inhibitors; NSAIDs may increase kidney risks. Contraindicated during pregnancy.
olderAdultSafety: Older adults may be more susceptible to dizziness and low blood pressure, especially when dehydrated or taking other blood pressure medicines. Monitor blood pressure, kidney function, and potassium, particularly after dose changes.
caregiverGuidance: Administer as prescribed and monitor blood pressure. Assist with slow position changes to reduce fall risk. Report fainting, unusual weakness, or reduced urine output. Avoid potassium supplements and salt substitutes unless approved, and consult the healthcare provider before using NSAIDs.

name: Terazosin Hydrochloride
usedFor: Treats hypertension and relieves urinary symptoms caused by benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), or an enlarged prostate.
howItWorks: Blocks alpha-1 receptors, relaxing blood vessels to lower blood pressure and relaxing muscles in the prostate and bladder neck to improve urine flow.
commonSideEffects: Dizziness, weakness, headache, drowsiness, nasal congestion, and blurred vision
adverseEffects: Severe postural hypotension, fainting, rapid heartbeat, allergic reactions, and priapism (prolonged, painful erection)
warnings: Start at a low dose, usually at bedtime, as prescribed. Monitor blood pressure, especially after the first dose or dose increases. Use caution with other antihypertensives and PDE5 inhibitors, such as tadalafil, due to increased hypotension risk. Inform the eye surgeon before cataract surgery.
olderAdultSafety: Generally avoid using terazosin as a first-line treatment for hypertension in older adults because of the risk of orthostatic hypotension and falls. Monitor closely for dizziness, fainting, and changes in blood pressure, especially when starting or restarting therapy.
caregiverGuidance: Give the first dose at bedtime if prescribed that way. Assist the patient when standing and encourage slow position changes. Monitor for dizziness or fainting, and report these symptoms to the healthcare provider. Seek emergency care for severe allergic reactions or a prolonged, painful erection.

name: Tolvaptan
drugClass: Selective vasopressin V2-receptor antagonist; aquaretic agent
usedFor: Treats certain cases of low blood sodium (hyponatremia), including those associated with heart failure or SIADH. Certain formulations are also used to slow kidney function decline in adults with rapidly progressing autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD).
howItWorks: Blocks vasopressin at the kidneys, increasing the excretion of free water while retaining electrolytes. This helps raise blood sodium levels or, in ADPKD, slow kidney disease progression.
commonSideEffects: Thirst, dry mouth, increased urination, frequent nighttime urination, and constipation
adverseEffects: Overly rapid sodium correction, severe dehydration, low blood volume, and serious liver injury
warnings: For hyponatremia, initiate or restart only in a hospital with close serum sodium monitoring. Monitor fluid balance, electrolytes, and kidney and liver function as appropriate. Avoid use in patients unable to sense thirst, with hypovolemic hyponatremia, or with anuria. Formulation-specific restrictions apply.
olderAdultSafety: Older adults may be more vulnerable to dehydration, electrolyte disturbances, and falls from frequent urination or dizziness. Monitor sodium levels, hydration, urine output, and kidney function closely.
caregiverGuidance: Administer exactly as prescribed. Monitor fluid intake and urine output as directed, and report excessive thirst, weakness, confusion, or reduced fluid intake. Report signs of liver injury, such as dark urine, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or persistent nausea. Do not independently restrict fluids or change the dose.

name: Torasemide
usedFor: Treats edema caused by heart failure, kidney disease, or liver disease. It is also used to treat hypertension.
howItWorks: Blocks sodium and chloride reabsorption in the kidneys, increasing the excretion of salt and water through urine. This reduces fluid buildup and may lower blood pressure.
commonSideEffects: Frequent urination, headache, dizziness, nausea, and diarrhea
adverseEffects: Severe dehydration, hypotension, electrolyte imbalance (especially low potassium), worsening kidney function, and hearing problems
warnings: Monitor blood pressure, fluid balance, kidney function, electrolytes, and blood glucose. Use cautiously in kidney or liver disease, diabetes, and gout. NSAIDs may reduce its effect and increase kidney risks. Avoid use in anuria or hepatic coma.
olderAdultSafety: Older adults may be more prone to dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, low blood pressure, and falls. Monitor weight, urine output, kidney function, and electrolyte levels, especially after dose changes.
caregiverGuidance: Administer as prescribed, preferably in the morning to reduce nighttime urination. Monitor weight and urine output as directed. Assist with slow position changes and report severe dizziness, muscle cramps, unusual weakness, reduced urination, or hearing changes. Do not change fluid or potassium intake without healthcare-provider guidance.

name: Urapidil
drugClass: Alpha-1 adrenergic blocker; centrally acting antihypertensive
usedFor: Treats hypertension. The intravenous formulation is used for severe hypertension or hypertensive emergencies in settings where it is approved.
howItWorks: Blocks alpha-1 receptors in blood vessels, reducing vascular resistance. It also acts centrally to reduce sympathetic activity, lowering blood pressure.
adverseEffects: Excessive hypotension, orthostatic hypotension, slow or rapid heartbeat, palpitations, and allergic reactions. Rarely, priapism or a decrease in platelet count may occur
warnings: Monitor blood pressure and heart rate closely, especially during IV administration. Use cautiously in liver or kidney impairment, dehydration, and certain heart conditions. Other antihypertensives, alpha-blockers, and alcohol may increase the risk of hypotension.
olderAdultSafety: Older adults may have slower drug clearance and increased sensitivity to blood pressure changes. A lower starting dose may be needed. Monitor for dizziness, postural hypotension, and falls.
caregiverGuidance: Administer as prescribed and monitor blood pressure. Assist with slow position changes to prevent falls. Report fainting, unusual weakness, palpitations, or allergic reactions. Avoid alcohol and consult the healthcare provider before combining it with other blood pressure medicines.

name: Valsartan
usedFor: Treats hypertension and heart failure. It also reduces cardiovascular mortality in clinically stable patients with left ventricular dysfunction after a heart attack.
howItWorks: Blocks angiotensin II receptors, preventing blood vessels from narrowing. This relaxes blood vessels, lowers blood pressure, and reduces the workload of the heart.
commonSideEffects: Dizziness, headache, fatigue, diarrhea, and abdominal pain
adverseEffects: Severe hypotension, hyperkalemia, kidney impairment, angioedema, and fetal harm during pregnancy
warnings: Monitor blood pressure, kidney function, and potassium levels. Use cautiously in dehydration or kidney disease. Avoid potassium supplements and potassium-containing salt substitutes unless approved. NSAIDs may increase kidney risks. Do not use during pregnancy. Avoid combining with aliskiren in patients with diabetes.
olderAdultSafety: Older adults may be more susceptible to dizziness, hypotension, and kidney impairment, especially with dehydration or other blood pressure medicines. Monitor blood pressure, kidney function, and potassium levels.
caregiverGuidance: Administer as prescribed and monitor blood pressure. Assist with slow position changes to prevent falls. Report fainting, unusual weakness, or reduced urine output. Avoid potassium supplements and salt substitutes unless approved, and consult the healthcare provider before taking NSAIDs.

name: Verapamil
drugClass: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker; antianginal; antiarrhythmic
usedFor: Treats hypertension, angina (chest pain), and certain abnormal heart rhythms, particularly supraventricular arrhythmias.
howItWorks: Blocks calcium entry into heart and blood vessel muscle cells. This relaxes blood vessels, lowers blood pressure, slows the heart rate, and reduces the heart's workload.
commonSideEffects: Constipation, dizziness, headache, nausea, and low blood pressure
adverseEffects: Severe bradycardia, heart block, worsening heart failure, and severe hypotension
warnings: Monitor blood pressure and heart rate. Use cautiously in heart failure, conduction disorders, and liver impairment. Combining with beta-blockers may increase the risk of severe bradycardia and heart block. Grapefruit may interact with some formulations.
olderAdultSafety: Older adults may be more sensitive to its effects and may have an increased risk of constipation, dizziness, hypotension, and slow heart rate. Monitor blood pressure, pulse, bowel habits, and signs of worsening heart failure.
caregiverGuidance: Administer as prescribed and monitor blood pressure and pulse. Assist with slow position changes to prevent falls. Encourage fiber-rich foods and adequate fluids if not restricted. Report fainting, an unusually slow heartbeat, swelling, or difficulty breathing. Do not stop the medication without consulting the healthcare provider.

name: Zofenopril
usedFor: Treats hypertension and may be used to treat acute myocardial infarction in eligible patients, depending on the approved product indication.
howItWorks: Blocks the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, helping blood vessels relax and reducing blood pressure and the workload of the heart.
commonSideEffects: Dizziness, headache, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and dry cough
adverseEffects: Angioedema, severe hypotension, hyperkalemia, kidney impairment, liver injury, and reduced white blood cell counts
warnings: Monitor blood pressure, kidney function, and potassium levels. Use cautiously in dehydration, kidney disease, and liver impairment. Avoid potassium supplements and salt substitutes unless approved. Do not use during pregnancy, and avoid combining with sacubitril/valsartan without the required washout period.
olderAdultSafety: Older adults may be more susceptible to low blood pressure, dizziness, and kidney impairment, especially with dehydration or diuretic use. Monitor blood pressure, kidney function, and potassium closely after starting treatment or adjusting the dose.
caregiverGuidance: prescribed and monitor blood pressure. Assist with slow position changes to reduce fall risk. Report persistent cough, unusual weakness, or reduced urine output. Seek emergency care for swelling of the face or throat or difficulty breathing.

name: Zofenopril Calcium
usedFor: Treats hypertension and may be used to treat acute myocardial infarction in eligible patients, depending on the approved product indication.
howItWorks: Blocks the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, helping blood vessels relax and reducing blood pressure and the workload of the heart.
commonSideEffects: Dizziness, headache, fatigue, cough, nausea, and gastrointestinal discomfort
adverseEffects: Angioedema, severe hypotension, hyperkalemia, kidney impairment, liver injury, and neutropenia
warnings: Monitor blood pressure, kidney function, and potassium. Use cautiously in kidney impairment or dehydration. Avoid potassium supplements and potassium-containing salt substitutes unless approved. Contraindicated during pregnancy and in patients with a history of ACE inhibitor-related angioedema. Do not combine with sacubitril/valsartan within 36 hours of switching.
olderAdultSafety: Older adults may be more susceptible to hypotension and kidney impairment, particularly with dehydration or diuretic use. Monitor blood pressure, renal function, and potassium after starting treatment or adjusting the dose.
caregiverGuidance: Administer as prescribed and monitor blood pressure. Assist with slow position changes to prevent falls. Report persistent cough, unusual weakness, or reduced urine output. Seek emergency help for swelling of the face, lips, or throat or difficulty breathing.
